database_metadata.name: AI-Driven Cyber Attack Progression Prediction System - Zeek-to-MITRE ATT&CK Mapping Database
database_metadata.description: Machine-readable Zeek telemetry to MITRE ATT&CK technique mapping database with structured correlation rules for behavioral detection.
schema_notes: All correlation rules are declarative, machine-readable, and SQL-free.
The generic correlation engine consumes correlation_rule fields directly.
Field names preserve original Zeek log field naming (conn.id.orig_h, etc.).
Endpoint confirmation is represented via external_context, not fabricated fields.
confidence_score represents mapping strength, not runtime detection confidence.

attack_technique.technique_name: Gather Victim Network Information: Domain Properties

evidence_conditions: DNS queries for MX, NS, SOA, or TXT records for a target domain
Queries originate from a non-DNS-server internal host
Multiple record types queried for the same domain in sequence
Queries for subdomains or wildcard patterns
mappings.false_positive_notes: Email servers, mail clients, and legitimate applications query MX records. DNS resolvers query NS records. The role of the originating host is important for distinguishing reconnaissance from legitimate DNS activity.
mappings.explanation: DNS reconnaissance for domain properties involves querying MX, NS, SOA, and TXT records to identify domain infrastructure. Zeek dns.log directly exposes qtype_name, allowing these queries to be detected at the event level.

external_context.notes: Source host location and role require asset inventory or network context. Temporal behavior involving multiple record types requires correlation across DNS events.

evidence_conditions: PTR queries for internal IP ranges
Queries for internal domain names from non-infrastructure hosts
Queries targeting internal DNS or NTP infrastructure
mappings.false_positive_notes: Applications and services commonly perform reverse DNS lookups. Confidence is moderate because a single PTR query is weak evidence without additional context.
mappings.explanation: Network configuration discovery may involve reverse DNS queries used to identify internal hosts and infrastructure. Zeek dns.log captures PTR queries and their target domains.

external_context.notes: Host classification and query target classification require external asset and network context. Internal IP range membership may also require network boundary configuration.

evidence_conditions: Zeek notice generated for a known exploit attempt
Notice indicates HTTP::SQL_Injection, HTTP::Shellshock, HTTP::APTSimulator, or another exploit-related category
Source is external and destination is an internal web server
Notice message contains exploit-specific indicators
mappings.false_positive_notes: Zeek notice detection can produce false positives for complex application behavior. Verification with application and endpoint telemetry is recommended.
mappings.explanation: Exploit-related Zeek notices provide strong network evidence of an attempted exploitation of a public-facing application.

external_context.notes: Source and destination network location require network boundary context. Destination role requires asset inventory.

evidence_conditions: HTTP request contains SQL injection, path traversal, or command injection patterns
Unusual HTTP methods such as PUT, DELETE, or PATCH
Large request body
HTTP 500 response following suspicious request
Suspicious or missing user agent

external_context.notes: Public-facing application classification requires network and asset context. Endpoint classification is not available directly from http.log.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate APIs, web application testing, search functionality, and content management systems may produce similar patterns.
mappings.explanation: HTTP exploitation attempts can be detected through suspicious URI patterns, HTTP methods, and server error responses. External-to-internal traffic targeting a known web server increases confidence.

evidence_conditions: HTTP protocol anomaly detected
Malformed HTTP request or invalid HTTP verb
Weird event targets a web server port

external_context.notes: Source and destination locations and destination server role require external context.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Broken clients, proxies, and malformed legitimate requests can generate protocol anomalies.
mappings.explanation: Protocol anomalies targeting an internal web server from an external source may indicate exploitation attempts.

evidence_conditions: External source connects to internal host on a remote access port
Remote access ports include SSH, RDP, VNC, and WinRM
Connection is established
Duration exceeds 60 seconds
mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate remote administration, VPN access, and third-party support are common.
mappings.explanation: External remote services can provide an initial access path. External-to-internal connections on remote administration ports provide direct network evidence.

external_context.notes: Internal/external classification requires network boundary configuration.

evidence_conditions: Successful SSH authentication
Source is external
Source is not a known VPN or administrative host
Source location is unexpected

external_context.notes: VPN, administrative-host, and geolocation classification require external context. Brute-force history requires temporal correlation.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Remote workers, VPN users, and third-party contractors may legitimately authenticate externally.
mappings.explanation: A successful SSH authentication from an unexpected external source can indicate use of compromised valid credentials.

evidence_conditions: RDP connection from external source to internal host
Connection is established
Duration exceeds 300 seconds
Source is not a known administrative host

external_context.notes: Network boundaries and administrative host classification require external context.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Remote desktop administration and remote workers commonly generate this traffic.
mappings.explanation: A sustained external RDP connection to an internal host may indicate use of valid compromised credentials, although Zeek cannot directly prove successful RDP authentication.

evidence_conditions: HTTP POST or PUT request uploads a file
Uploaded file has a script or executable extension
Upload endpoint is not a known legitimate upload endpoint
Upload succeeds
Filename extension and MIME type are inconsistent
mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate CMS uploads, document repositories, and development systems can upload executable-looking files.
mappings.explanation: Uploading a server-side script to a web application can indicate web shell placement. Zeek can observe the HTTP request and transferred file metadata.

external_context.notes: Web-server classification and upload endpoint legitimacy require application and asset inventory context.

evidence_conditions: Internal host downloads an executable, script, archive, or tool
Downloaded file has a suspicious extension
HTTP response is 200
File transfer is confirmed by files.log

external_context.notes: Internal/external network classification requires network boundary context. Execution requires endpoint telemetry and is not inferred from the download alone.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Software updates, package managers, browser downloads, and enterprise deployment systems can produce similar transfers.
mappings.explanation: Zeek can observe file transfers but cannot determine whether the downloaded tool was subsequently executed.

evidence_conditions: Executable file downloaded through HTTP
MIME type indicates executable content
File extension is executable
Destination is an internal workstation

external_context.notes: Destination host classification requires asset inventory. Threat-intelligence hash checking is external enrichment rather than an event-level condition.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate software downloads, installers, and updates can match these conditions.
mappings.explanation: Executable files transferred to internal workstations can provide evidence of possible client-side exploitation or malware delivery.

evidence_conditions: Browser downloads potentially executable content
Referrer is present
User-Agent indicates browser activity
Downloaded file has an executable or script extension

external_context.notes: Domain reputation requires threat-intelligence or reputation enrichment. Actual user execution cannot be established from Zeek HTTP telemetry alone.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate downloads and user-initiated file transfers are common.
mappings.explanation: Zeek can observe a suspicious file download that may precede user execution, but cannot directly prove that the user executed the file.

evidence_conditions: HTTP download of command scripts
Download originates from an external server
HTTP response is 200
File metadata confirms script transfer

external_context.notes: Network location classification requires external network context.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Administrative scripts, software deployment systems, and automation frameworks may legitimately transfer scripts.
mappings.explanation: Zeek detects transfer of script files but cannot confirm their execution.

evidence_conditions: RDP connection between internal hosts
Established RDP session
Duration exceeds 60 seconds
Significant bidirectional traffic

external_context.notes: Internal host classification and typical RDP client role require asset inventory.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate remote administration and help desk activity can produce this pattern.
mappings.explanation: RDP between internal hosts can represent lateral movement. Source and destination host context helps distinguish administrative activity from anomalous movement.

evidence_conditions: SMB connection between internal hosts
Connection is established
Source is a workstation
Source connects to administrative servers

external_context.notes: Host locations and source role require asset inventory. SMB share names require SMB protocol telemetry and are not available from conn.log alone.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Normal file-server access and administrative activity can produce SMB connections.
mappings.explanation: SMB connections on port 445 provide network evidence associated with Windows lateral movement, but conn.log alone cannot prove access to ADMIN$ or C$ shares.

evidence_conditions: Successful SSH authentication between internal hosts
Source host is not a typical SSH client
Source subsequently connects to additional internal hosts

external_context.notes: Host locations and source role require asset inventory. Subsequent connections require temporal correlation.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate administration, automation, and developer access may generate successful internal SSH sessions.
mappings.explanation: Successful SSH authentication between internal hosts is consistent with lateral movement, especially when the source host is not normally used for SSH administration.

evidence_conditions: HTTP GET downloads an executable or script
HTTP response is 200
Downloaded file is larger than 10 KB
File extension or MIME type indicates executable content

external_context.notes: Network location requires network boundary context. Suspicious activity preceding the transfer requires temporal correlation.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate software downloads and updates can produce similar traffic.
mappings.explanation: HTTP downloads of executable or script content from external hosts can indicate ingress tool transfer.

evidence_conditions: FTP RETR command downloads an executable or script
Transfer succeeds with reply code 226
File is larger than 10 KB
Transfer is from an external FTP server

external_context.notes: Network location requires network boundary context.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate FTP software and data transfers may produce similar events.
mappings.explanation: FTP RETR commands downloading executable or script files from external servers provide evidence of ingress tool transfer.
